name: Ash rose
lede: Ash Rose greys the pink of the rose flower toward the color of cold ash, a combination ColorHub's library traces only to a Japanese color list, not to an English dictionary.

sections.title: Rose cooled toward ash
sections.body:
Rose is the flower; "ash" here describes the cool grey cast, as if the pink had been dusted with cold ash from a fire [1]. ColorHub's library carries this exact name from a Japanese color list, with no separate English-language first record in the sources consulted; who coined the English name, or when, is undocumented here [1]. In printed English the phrase rose fastest in the 1980s and peaked in the 2010s, well after any pigment record [2]. Its closest named neighbors are [[antique-rose|Deep Vinaceous]] and [[antique-rose|Antique Rose]], a near-twin at ΔE 4.4, with [[old-rose|Old Rose]] a lighter relative nearby [3].

ColorHub's Japanese-sourced library entries sit alongside many English rose variants without always lining up on a coining date; the lack of an English record here does not mean the color is only Japanese, only that no earlier English source turned up in the sources consulted [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds Ash Rose in 87 of 23,781 paintings (0.37 percent, as photographed), rarer than 53 percent of named colors here [4]. It most often sits as a hidden color, found that way in 51 percent of the paintings where it dominates, and is over-represented in Indian paintings (2.5 times expected) [4]. The earliest matching canvas dates to the year 1000, among the oldest in the archive; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first, though no large age gap to the name's record shows up here regardless [4]. That hidden-color role, more than any other, is what separates it from brighter named pinks: it tends to sit in shaded folds of cloth rather than catching the light [4]. As with other dulled rose names in our library, that recurrence is only a hue match, not evidence that any painter thought of their mixture as Ash Rose [4].
